title: Gigantic DapuStor R6060 512TB E2 NVMe SSD Shown at FMS 2026
gist: At FMS 2026, DapuStor showed a 512TB E2-form-factor NVMe SSD (2x the ~256TB ceiling of E3.S/U.2 drives), even as the show's second big storyline is a broader industry pullback from the years-long trend of ever-increasing SSD capacities, driven by rising NAND costs.

insights.claim: FMS 2026 is notably more upbeat than the prior year's show, with NAND and DRAM vendors experiencing unprecedented business booms.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signals a demand/pricing upcycle for memory and storage suppliers worth tracking across NAND/DRAM vendor earnings and guidance.
insights.quote: the show is significantly more upbeat, with many NAND and DRAM vendors experiencing unprecedented business booms

insights.claim: Despite the historical trend of relentlessly increasing SSD capacities, FMS 2026 shows a notable shift away from that trend, according to the author's second major storyline of the show.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A pause in capacity scaling at the high end is a leading indicator for storage vendors' roadmaps and for hyperscaler procurement strategy shifting toward cost-per-TB over raw density.
insights.quote: there is a notable shift away from the trend of ever-increasing SSD capacities
insights.locator: Second, there is a notable shift

insights.claim: Rising NAND pricing has made total system cost so heavily dictated by the NAND itself that it now makes more economic sense to deploy smaller-capacity drives rather than continuing to push maximum capacity per drive.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Explains the capacity-growth deceleration as a NAND-pricing effect, not a technology ceiling; watch NAND spot/contract pricing as the variable that will reverse this once it eases.
insights.quote: as NAND pricing increased, the system’s cost is now so heavily dictated by NAND that it makes sense to use smaller-capacity drives
insights.locator: What has happened in the meantime

insights.claim: The DapuStor R6060 512TB E2 NVMe SSD is notably larger than higher-end E3.S or U.2 drives, which are topping out around 256TB.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Marks E2 as the form factor now leading the capacity frontier in enterprise NVMe SSDs, relevant for datacenter storage architects evaluating density-per-slot.
insights.quote: This is a 512TB model, making it notably larger than the higher-end E3.S or U.2 drives that are pushing 256TB capacities.

insights.claim: In DapuStor's own Roealsen6 lineup, the E3.L and E1.L form factors are capacity-limited to roughly 256TB (245.76TB), while only the E2 form factor reaches 512TB.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Confirms E2's physical depth/width advantage translates directly into a 2x capacity ceiling versus competing EDSFF form factors from the same vendor.
insights.quote: For form factors like E3.L and E1.L the capacity is limited to 256TB (245.76TB)

insights.claim: The E2 form factor lets a server attach more storage capacity to a given single- or dual-CPU host, which lowers the cost of bringing storage online because fewer chassis, motherboards, and memory modules are needed per petabyte.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A structural TCO argument for E2 over denser-chassis alternatives (e.g., 2U E3.L servers): fewer host systems per PB compresses capex and, if power-optimized, opex too.
insights.quote: the E2 form factor allows you to attach more capacity to a given CPU or dual CPU server.

insights.claim: Because the E2 form factor has more NAND placement sites, it can also be used to hit lower capacity points using lower-density NAND, which may help vendors deliver lower-cost SSDs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Gives E2 flexibility as both a max-density and a cost-optimization form factor, potentially widening its addressable use cases beyond hyperscale bulk storage.
insights.quote: E2 also allows you to hit a lower capacity with lower-density NAND because you have more NAND sites, which may help deliver lower-cost SSDs.

insights.claim: A server with 36 E2 drive bays populated with 512TB DapuStor R6060 drives would provide 16PB of capacity in a single system.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete density benchmark for hyperscale storage-node planning: a single E2 chassis can now reach 16PB, reducing rack-level node count for a given capacity target.
insights.quote: a 512TB drive allows you to have a single system with 16PB of capacity.
insights.locator: Even if you look at the server below

insights.claim: High-capacity QLC NAND is in demand because use cases like storing training data for models, handling inference cache reads, and storing video/audio content are driving storage capacity needs more than raw performance needs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reframes enterprise SSD demand: AI training/inference and media workloads are now capacity-bound, not IOPS-bound, favoring QLC-based high-capacity drives over performance-tier SLC/TLC parts.
insights.quote: High-capacity QLC NAND is in demand these days because simply holding enough training data for modern models, handling cache reads in inference, storing video and audio
insights.locator: High-capacity QLC NAND is in demand

insights.claim: DapuStor did not disclose pricing for the R6060 512TB E2 SSD at FMS 2026, and the author expects it to be expensive given current NAND pricing conditions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: No public price point yet means true cost-per-TB economics of E2 at 512TB remain unverified; watch for follow-up pricing disclosures before drawing procurement conclusions.
insights.quote: We did not get an exact figure, but I would expect it to be a lot given current NAND pricing.
